bumblebees (bombus terrestris) are capable of context-dependent, centrally controlled reduction of nocifensive behavior, demonstrating that they can modulate their avoidance of noxious heat (55°c) based on the availability of alternative food rewards [12].

when unheated feeders contained high sucrose concentrations (40%), bees significantly avoided noxiously heated feeders; however, as the sucrose concentration at unheated feeders decreased (to 10%, 20%, or 30%), bees progressively increased their feeding from the heated feeders, demonstrating a motivational trade-off [12].

bees used learned color cues associated with feeder quality to make foraging decisions, indicating that the motivational trade-off was mediated by central nervous system processing and associative memory, rather than solely by peripheral sensory input [12].

the study employed a motivational trade-off paradigm in which 41 forager bees from eight colonies were tested across two temperature conditions (unheated vs. heated feeders at 55°c) and four sucrose concentration levels (10%, 20%, 30%, or 40%) to assess flexible decision-making under competing motivations [12].

the authors conclude that while the observed ability of bumblebees to modulate nociceptive behavior based on contextual information is consistent with a capacity for pain experiences in insects, the subjective nature of pain means this finding does not constitute formal proof, though it supports applying the precautionary principle in insect welfare considerations [12].

klein and barron [4] argue that phenomenal consciousness is a consequence of how mobile animals with spatial senses and a capacity for goal-directed behaviour resolve the complex problem of action selection.

according to klein and barron [4], brains solve action selection problems by transforming heterogeneous information—including sensory inputs, representations of internal state, and stored knowledge of values—into a common framework called a "phenomenal interface" to compute multi-objective q-values.

in insects, the central complex and mushroom bodies operate together as a system to constitute the phenomenal interface, with the central complex responsible for correcting for self-motion in order to hold a heading towards a goal [4].

klein and barron [4] suggest that possession of a phenomenal interface naturally gives rise to key features of subjectivity, including a first-person perspective in which external stimuli have a subjective value.

the authors extend merker's subcortical theory of phenomenal consciousness by demonstrating that analogues of the key neural systems emphasized by merker occur in arthropods, supporting the possibility of basal consciousness in insects [4].

the authors propose that insects possess a capacity for subjective experience, which represents the most basic aspect of consciousness—defined as there being "something it is like" for the organism to be aware of the world barron and klein [1].

in vertebrates, the capacity for subjective experience is supported by integrated midbrain structures (including the tectum/superior colliculus and hypothalamus) that create a unified neural simulation of the animal's mobile body within its environment barron and klein [1].

the insect central complex (cx) performs functions analogous to the vertebrate tectum/colliculus by processing multiple sources of spatial information (visual, mechanosensory, and proprioceptive) and encoding the insect's heading relative to environmental landmarks [1].

the paper argues that the origins of subjective experience can be traced to the cambrian period (~500 million years ago), based on fossil evidence that basal vertebrates and arthropods from this era possessed the neural structures necessary for a behavioral "core control system" [1].

the authors distinguish primary consciousness (the capacity for subjective experience) from higher-order forms of consciousness such as self-reflexive or access consciousness, and they contend that while insects likely possess the former, it is "exceedingly unlikely" they possess the latter [1].

the paper proposes a tripartite taxonomy of human consciousness: autonoetic (explicit self-awareness of one's existence over time), noetic (explicit awareness of facts and concepts about the world or oneself), and anoetic (implicit/tacit awareness of one's self and the world in the moment) [28].

tulving's scheme associates each kind of consciousness with a distinct kind of empirically measurable memory: autonoetic consciousness with episodic memory; noetic consciousness with semantic and conceptual memory; and anoetic consciousness with procedural memory [28].

the best measure of consciousness is verbal self-report, because people can respond verbally or non-verbally to something they are conscious of but can only respond non-verbally to something they are not conscious of [28].
the circuits underlying the conscious experience of fear operate in parallel with the reflex-like behavioural and physiological control circuits that operate non-consciously [28].

the lateral frontal pole, a region of the anterior frontal cortex that is lacking in other primates, has been specifically implicated in episodic cognition and autonoetic consciousness in humans [28].
